opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about it less than you might expect, and I've come to think that's mostly a healthy thing. Almost everything I've worked on that I'm proud of has been deeply collaborative, with students, with colleagues, with people I've never met whose papers I read at exactly the right moment. So if you ask "whose idea was this?" for any given project, the honest answer is usually that it emerged out of a lot of conversations, and trying to carve out my individual contribution would be a little artificial.

Where I do think about credit is in terms of the people I work with, especially students. Academia still runs on a fairly individualistic reputation economy: people get hired, get fellowships, get tenure based on being legible as the person behind some line of work. So part of my job as an advisor is making sure that the students who actually did the hard thinking and the hard engineering get recognized for it, that they're the ones giving the talks, that their names are attached to the ideas. I'd much rather the lab's influence show up as a bunch of people going on to do their own interesting things than as my name on a lot of citations.

In terms of influence more broadly, the thing I find most satisfying isn't when someone builds directly on a specific paper. It's when a way of framing a problem kind of diffuses into the field, when people start asking a question that wasn't being asked before, even if they've forgotten or never knew where it came from. That kind of influence is almost by definition hard to attribute, and I think that's fine. If the point is to understand language and learning better, it doesn't really matter whose name is on the understanding.

The flip side is that I try to be a little skeptical of chasing influence directly. It's easy in a fast-moving field to optimize for being first, or for the flashy result, and I think that tends to produce worse science. I'd rather work on questions that I think are genuinely interesting and important and trust that, if the work is good, it'll find the people it needs to find.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it matters more to understand language and learning than whose name is attached, and favors collective progress over individual recognition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it less than I probably should, honestly. The honest answer is that almost everything I've worked on that turned out to matter was something a lot of other people were circling at the same time. Neural module networks are a good example. When we were doing that work, there were groups at Berkeley, at Stanford, at Facebook, all converging on this idea that you could compose neural components according to some kind of linguistic structure. If we hadn't written that paper, somebody else would have written a very similar one within a year. So it's hard for me to look at that and say, this was my contribution, as opposed to, I happened to be standing in a particular place when a particular idea became obvious.

That said, I don't think the right conclusion is that individual work doesn't matter. The thing I actually care about is whether a specific framing or a specific way of asking a question ends up in other people's heads. The citations are a very noisy proxy for that. What I'd rather see is a student at some other university building on an idea in a direction I wouldn't have thought of, or someone in a totally different subfield picking up a formalism because it happened to be the right tool. That's the kind of influence that feels real to me, and it's mostly invisible in the usual metrics.

The other thing I've come to believe, partly from advising, is that the biggest effect I have is probably not through papers at all. It's through the students I work with and the taste they develop about what problems are worth working on. If someone leaves my group with good judgment about what's interesting and what's a dead end, that compounds over decades in a way that no single paper does. So when I think about credit, I try to hold it pretty loosely and think more about whether the research community is collectively asking better questions than it was a few years ago.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they hold credit loosely and care more about whether the research community is asking better questions, placing collective progress above individual recognition.

astra-6.text:
I think individual credit is tricky, because the research you do is shaped by so many people. There are the people you collaborate with directly, but also people who ask a good question or introduce you to a way of thinking about a problem. Those influences don’t always show up in an author list.

I try to be specific about who contributed what, and to acknowledge the ideas that a project builds on. Authorship matters, especially for people early in their careers. But I’m hesitant to tell a story where a piece of research comes entirely from one person. Often the interesting thing is how several people’s perspectives came together.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes shared influences and resists attributing research to one person, but it does not say that advancing collective knowledge matters more than receiving credit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think individual credit is tricky because research is such a collective enterprise. You can sometimes point to a particular idea and say who first articulated it, but that idea usually depends on conversations, tools, and earlier work from a lot of other people. And even within a project, the person who has the initial idea isn’t necessarily the person who figures out what makes it work or what it actually means.

So I try to be specific about contributions and generous about acknowledging them. Influence is even harder to measure. A paper might influence how someone frames a problem without ever becoming a citation, and a conversation with a student can matter more than something you publish. I’d like to think about influence in terms of whether we’ve helped other people ask better questions and do work they couldn’t have done before.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as collective and urges generous acknowledgment, but it does not clearly say that advancing collective knowledge matters more than who receives credit.
